text:
The sea dragon lowered herself around the hatchling, curving her great body between it and the storm. She folded one wing over the little dragon. The hatchling pressed close beneath it, safe and dry.

Ekin and Duru watched mother and hatchling settle together. Neither girl moved until the hatchling’s trembling stopped.

Thunder shook the upper room. Ekin looked toward the open door, then out into the rain. Somewhere beyond the headland and the dark sea, her grandfather’s brass compass was gone beyond recovery.

“I kept thinking I could still get it back,” she said. Her voice tightened, but she did not turn away. “I can’t. The compass is lost.”

Duru watched Ekin accept the words and the hurt behind them. “We should take the coastal path before the rain gets worse.”

Ekin’s first answer rose sharp in her throat. She swallowed it. Duru had guided her safely before, and Ekin chose to listen now.

“All right,” Ekin said. “You lead.”

Duru stepped through the open upper-room door and reached the coastal path.

Ekin stepped through the open upper-room door and reached the coastal path.

They set off together along the established coastal route toward the harbor. The storm continued throughout their return. Rain swept across the path, and thunder rolled over the sea. Both girls saw the storm still raging and kept close enough to watch each other’s footing.

When the harbor came into view, Duru followed the established coastal path and reached the harbor.

Ekin followed the established coastal path and reached the harbor.

They stood there together, soaked and tired. Ekin glanced back toward the distant lighthouse. The compass would not return, and she would not pretend its loss did not matter. Then she faced Duru.

“I’m glad I didn’t do all of that alone,” she said.

Duru gave a small nod. It was not the ease of old friendship, but it was trust they had earned.
